newsitem.title: POLAND: Polish NBP again tightens reins on robust economy.
newsitem.headline: Polish NBP again tightens reins on robust economy.

text.p: The National Bank of Poland (NBP) has tightened monetary policy further to cool the country's domestic demand-driven economy but it faces an uphill battle to curb corporate credit growth, analysts said on Tuesday.
Last Friday the NBP said that from April 30 it would raise reserves on long-term zloty deposits by two points to 11 percent and foreign currency deposits by one to five percent.
The central bank said it was raising obligatory reserves to further limit credit expansion, reduce internal demand and curb the widening trade deficit.

"Consumption credit growth has slowed because of the tight monetary policy, but it will be hard to cool corporate credit as the economy is booming and demand is larger than output," said Adam Czyzewski, analyst at the independent NOBE institute.
Poland's economic growth, fuelled by fast growing internal demand, has created a rapidly swelling trade gap as more and more Poles buy consumer goods, many of which were imported.

Poland's gross domestic product (GDP) may have grown as much as eight percent year-on-year in the first quarter after a six percent rise in 1996, as manufacturing continued to rise quickly despite higher costs of credit.
The steep first quarter inflation which slowed to year-on-year 16.6 percent in March from 18.5 in December made the GDP growth even more impressive.
Analysts said banks would now face a choice of whether to offset the higher costs stemming from higher reserves by raising credit or lowering deposit rates.

"Competition between banks for clients would likely keep deposit rates underpinned and force banks to rise credit rates, just as the NBP would like them to," said Andrzej Ladko, chief dealer at Bank Handlowy SA.

Credit in the economy increased nine percent in the January-April 10 period, with credit to households, which accounts for 18 percent of credit in nominal terms, increasing 11.1 percent in the period after more than doubling in 1996.

The central bank in February previously increased reserves to slow the fast expansion of credit action. It raised zloty call deposits by three points to 20 percent and doubled them on foreign currency deposits to four percent.
But the February rise failed to significantly slow credit growth partly because it began from a very low base and because of the steady growth of real wages, analysts said.

"We have had a big increase in credit but it has come from a low base in absolute terms, so it's not that we are actually seeing the economy bubble over or overheat," said Tim Harris, economist at Societe Generale in London.

They said the central bank may have chosen to increase required reserves instead of nominal interest rates, now at 25 percent for the lombard and 22 percent for the discount rate, to discourage short-term foreign capital inflows.
"An interest rate rise would spark even more inflows of speculative foreign capital, so the central bank may have decided to increase reserves instead," NOBE's Czyzewski said.
Analysts said higher reserves would reduce banks' liquidity and could limit central bank drainages and NBP-bill sales.
"The increased reserves could push up market rates, while limiting the scope of central bank open market operations, as funds flow out of the banking system," Handlowy's Ladko said.
Analysts said the move to boost reserves would not be followed by increases in the central bank's drainage rates.
"The central bank has shown that it was not willing to increase yields on its longer-term NBP-bills and it is likely to be consistent," said an analyst at a foreign firm in Warsaw.
